g.text: Same week, but not equally tight: 100% down to 53%
One dot: one genus starting on one night
Spawning: corals release eggs and sperm into the water
Genus: a group of closely related species
Spawning night: one genus on one reef on one date
Lunar month: 29.5 days, from full moon to full moon

Percentages: share of a genus’s nights inside the white frame (an even spread gives 27%). Tight: packed into few days. Bright pink: Pocillopora (cauliflower corals), split by sea after seeing the data. Waves smoothed by about a day.

Shown: the 12 genera with 40+ nights, of 48 recorded. Red Sea wave: 10 nights, 6 spawning events, 3 sites, 2 studies, all within 2 days of new moon, as in Bouwmeester et al. (2021). Platygyra has a small new-moon peak (19%).

Dots: 1,482 timed starts, some approximate. Of exact times in other genera, 97% fall in the 6 h after sunset. Daytime starts in other genera: 4 of 1,460. Sunrise comes about 12 h after sunset, varying by place and season.

Gaps in tightness mostly reflect where a genus was recorded: shuffling genus labels within reefs finds no clear gap without Eilat (p = 0.25). Records show when people looked, not every night. Source: Baird et al. (2021).
Eleven genera peak in the week after full moon and start around sunset.
Pocillopora spawns by day, and in the Red Sea at new moon.
Most coral genera share one timetable. Pocillopora does not
